questions.q: Define endogamy and exogamy in the context of the Indian caste system. Give one example of each.
questions.a: Endogamy: marriage within one's own caste/sub-caste (e.g., a Jat marrying a Jat). Exogamy: marriage outside one's gotra/clan/village (e.g., a Sharma gotra Brahmin cannot marry another Sharma gotra Brahmin). A wrong answer that swaps the definitions or gives only caste-level examples for both reveals confusion about the two levels at which these rules operate — endogamy at the caste boundary, exogamy at the kinship boundary.

questions.q: Explain the difference between hypergamy (anuloma) and hypogamy (pratiloma) in your own words. Why is hypogamy traditionally stigmatised in Dharmashastric texts?
questions.a: Hypergamy: woman marries a man of equal or higher ritual status (e.g., Brahmin woman → Kshatriya man). Hypogamy: woman marries a man of lower ritual status (e.g., Kshatriya woman → Vaishya man). Hypogamy is stigmatised because it lowers the woman's ritual status and that of her offspring, threatening the purity hierarchy. A wrong answer that defines them only in economic terms (dowry, wealth) misses the ritual-status dimension central to the classical texts.

questions.q: A Reddy (dominant caste) man from Andhra Pradesh marries a Brahmin woman. Identify which marriage rules are followed and which are violated. Justify using the concepts of endogamy, exogamy, hypergamy, hypogamy.
questions.a: Caste endogamy is violated (intercaste marriage). Gotra exogamy may be followed if their gotras differ. This is hypergamy (anuloma) because the woman (Brahmin, higher ritual status) marries a man of lower ritual status (Reddy, though politically/economically dominant). A wrong answer that calls this hypogamy because the Reddy is economically powerful confuses ritual status with secular power — a classic competitive-exam trap.

questions.q: Compare how endogamy and exogamy function together to maintain caste boundaries. Why does the caste system need both rules simultaneously?
questions.a: Endogamy keeps the caste group closed (no inflow/outflow of members), preserving ritual purity and occupational monopoly. Exogamy (gotra/village) prevents incest and creates affinal alliances *outside* the kinship unit but *inside* the caste. Together they ensure: (1) caste reproduction through endogamous marriages, (2) social network expansion through exogamous links. A wrong answer that treats them as contradictory fails to see they operate at different levels of social organisation.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "Modern education and urbanisation have made hypergamy irrelevant in India." Use sociological evidence to support your position.
questions.a: The statement is partially true but oversimplified. Education/urbanisation have weakened *caste-based* hypergamy (e.g., intercaste marriages rising), but *class-based* hypergamy persists (women still tend to marry men with equal/higher education/income). Matrimonial ads still highlight "well-settled groom" — a secular avatar of hypergamy. A wrong answer that says "hypergamy has disappeared" ignores the transformation of status criteria from ritual to socioeconomic.

questions.q: Construct a hypothetical matrimonial advertisement that simultaneously reflects caste endogamy, gotra exogamy, and hypergamy. Annotate each line with the rule it illustrates.
questions.a: Example: "Alliance invited for Kanyakubja Brahmin boy, 30, IAS (UP cadre). Caste: Brahmin only (endogama). Gotra: Not Kaushik, Vatsa (exogamy). Girl should be graduate, homely (hypergamy — status equivalence sought)." A poor answer lists rules without a coherent ad or misses one rule, showing inability to synthesise the three layers in a real-world context.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Marriage rules in India are culturally prescribed norms that regulate spouse selection: endogamy requires marrying within one's own social group (caste, sub-caste, religion); exogamy prohibits marriage within certain kinship units (gotra, clan, village); hypergamy (anuloma) prescribes that a woman marries a man of equal or higher ritual status; hypogamy (pratiloma) occurs when a woman marries a man of lower ritual status, ______ stigmatised.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are scrolling through a ______ website and see a profile that reads: "Seeking alliance for Brahmin boy, 28, Engineer.
What is Marriage rules in India? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Marriage rules in India are culturally prescribed norms that regulate spouse selection: endogamy requires marrying within one's own social group (caste, sub-caste, religion); exogamy prohibits marriage within certain kinship units (gotra, clan, village); hypergamy (anuloma) prescribes that a woman marries a man of equal or higher ritual.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Marriage rules in India?
questions.a: Students often think hypergamy means "dowry-giving" and hypogamy means "dowry-receiving", confusing economic transactions with ritual status rules.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) distinguish all four rules with precise Indian examples, (2) explain how endogamy and exogamy operate simultaneously in the caste system, (3) analyse how hypergamy/hypogamy reflect gendered status hierarchies, and (4) evaluate recent trends (e.g., intercaste marriages, love marriages) against these traditional rules.
